Fort Lauderdale Vacation Guide 2026: Hotels & Rentals

Fort Lauderdale Vacation Guide 2026: Quick Overview

Fort Lauderdale is a beach-and-waterway city on Florida's southeast coast. It's known for seven miles of public beach, more than 165 miles of navigable canals, and Las Olas Boulevard, the boutique-lined strip that anchors downtown. For a 2026 trip, we suggest picking one of two bases: a canal-front or beachfront vacation rental if you want space and privacy, or one of the oceanfront hotels along A1A if you want full-service amenities and beach access right outside your door. Both put you a short drive from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), the Everglades, and the calmer beach towns of Lauderdale-by-the-Sea and Pompano Beach.

This guide is built for travelers staying in Fort Lauderdale, not sailing out of it. If you're departing from nearby Port Everglades, we cover itineraries, terminals, and transfer logistics separately in our best cruise itineraries from Fort Lauderdale and Miami guide, and we'll point you back there at the end of this article. Everyone else, keep reading for where to sleep, where to walk, and how to structure a few days in one of Florida's more underrated coastal cities.

We wrote this from the perspective of a repeat visitor, not someone skimming brochures for the first time. Fort Lauderdale rewards travelers who slow down: a morning on Las Olas, an afternoon on a water taxi, an evening watching the sun drop over the Intracoastal from a dockside table. The neighborhoods here differ enough in character that picking the right base matters more than it does in most Florida beach towns, and that choice should drive whether you book a rental home or a hotel room.

Getting to Fort Lauderdale: FLL Airport Travel Tips

Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) sits roughly three miles south of downtown, which makes it a remarkably convenient airport for a beach vacation. Domestic arrivals typically land at Terminal 1, 2, or 3, while Terminal 4 handles most international flights, including connections to the Caribbean and Latin America. The terminals sit along a single loop road, so we'd suggest confirming yours before arranging ground transportation. A pickup booked for the wrong terminal can eat fifteen to twenty minutes of your first hour in Florida.

Rideshare and taxi lines at FLL can run long on peak cruise-season mornings. That's true even for travelers who have nothing to do with cruising, since Port Everglades traffic spills over into the airport's rideshare lots. If you want a guaranteed, no-wait pickup with a driver tracking your flight, book ahead through a dedicated Fort Lauderdale airport car service rather than queuing curbside, especially if you're arriving with golf clubs, dive gear, or a family of five and a mountain of luggage. A private black car or SUV also makes sense if your rental home or hotel is north in Lauderdale-by-the-Sea or Pompano Beach; those drives run twenty-five to forty minutes depending on traffic along Federal Highway or I-95.

Once you're settled, a car is genuinely optional if you base yourself downtown or along the beach corridor near Las Olas. The Sun Trolley and the Fort Lauderdale Water Taxi cover most of the tourist core, and Uber or Lyft fill the gaps. Travelers heading to the Everglades or up to Pompano's quieter shoreline will still want a rental car or a pre-booked private driver for the day.

Fort Lauderdale's Best Beach Neighborhoods: Choosing Your Base

Fort Lauderdale isn't one beach so much as a string of connected beach towns, each with its own personality. The central Fort Lauderdale Beach strip, along Highway A1A between Las Olas Boulevard and Sunrise Boulevard, is the liveliest stretch: the widest sidewalk promenade, the heaviest hotel density, and the closest walk to nightlife and restaurants. Most first-time visitors should stay here if walkability is the priority.

North of downtown, Lauderdale-by-the-Sea moves at a slower pace, built around El Mar Drive, a low-rise strip of boutique motels, dive shops, and casual seafood spots a few blocks from Anglin's Fishing Pier. We consistently point travelers here when they want beach mornings without beach-town crowds, and snorkelers love it thanks to a nearshore reef just a short swim out. Parking is easier than downtown, and the crowd skews toward couples and retirees rather than spring-break energy.

Keep heading north and you'll reach Pompano Beach, home to the Pompano Beach Pier and, just beyond it, the red-and-white Hillsboro Inlet Lighthouse, one of the tallest lighthouses in Florida and still an active aid to navigation. Pompano has poured money into its beachfront lately, with a redesigned pier plaza and a growing restaurant scene, and it remains noticeably cheaper than downtown Fort Lauderdale for both rentals and hotels.

South of the city, Hollywood Beach deserves its own trip even if you're not sleeping there. The Hollywood Beach Broadwalk is a 2.5-mile paved oceanfront promenade popular with cyclists, rollerbladers, and evening strollers, lined with open-air cafes and small hotels. It has a distinctly different, more old-Florida feel than Fort Lauderdale proper, and it makes an easy half-day trip from anywhere along the central beach corridor.

Las Olas Boulevard and Fort Lauderdale's Canal System

Las Olas Boulevard is Fort Lauderdale's signature street, a roughly one-mile stretch running from downtown to the beach and lined with independent boutiques, art galleries, and a dense cluster of restaurants that range from casual raw bars to white-tablecloth steakhouses. Plan at least one dinner here no matter where you're staying. The street is at its best in early evening, when outdoor tables fill up and the palm-lined median takes on a string-light glow.

What makes Fort Lauderdale genuinely unusual, though, sits just off Las Olas: a network of finger-island canals so extensive the city has long marketed itself as the Venice of America. Fort Lauderdale maintains more than 165 miles of navigable waterways, more than any other coastal city its size in the country, and much of that network is visible from the Las Olas Isles, a residential district of canal-front homes with private docks just south of the boulevard.

The easiest way to see it all is the Fort Lauderdale Water Taxi, a hop-on, hop-off service running along the New River and the Intracoastal Waterway, connecting downtown, Las Olas, the beach, and points south toward Hollywood. A day or multi-day water taxi pass is one of the better values in the city, and it doubles as sightseeing since the route passes yachts, mega-mansions, and working boatyards that explain why Fort Lauderdale calls itself the yachting capital of the world. For an evening on Las Olas without the hassle of parking, many visitors also book a private chauffeured car service for dinner transfers, sidestepping the valet lines that build up along the boulevard on weekend nights.

Fort Lauderdale Vacation Rentals: Best Options for Your Stay

A vacation rental tends to be the better choice for families, groups of friends, or anyone staying five nights or longer in Fort Lauderdale, at least in our experience. Canal-front homes in the Las Olas Isles and Rio Vista neighborhoods routinely come with private docks, heated pools, and outdoor kitchens, and they put you within a short walk or water taxi ride of both downtown and the beach. North of downtown, Lauderdale-by-the-Sea and Pompano Beach offer more budget-friendly rental inventory, including condos and townhomes a block or two from the sand that tend to run noticeably cheaper per night than comparable properties on the central beach strip.

Booking early matters more in Fort Lauderdale than most travelers expect. The city's calendar is packed with boat shows, marathons, and festivals that can absorb rental inventory months out, particularly the Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show each fall. We'd recommend filtering for private pools if you're traveling with kids or a large group, since Florida's afternoon thunderstorms between June and September can throw off beach plans, and a private pool keeps the day salvageable either way.

For families who want a private pool, a full kitchen, and enough bedrooms to keep everyone comfortable, start your search where you can browse Fort Lauderdale vacation rentals with pools on Vrbo, filtering by neighborhood and walk-to-beach distance. If your group's needs run more specific, say dock access for a boat, a pet-friendly listing, or a home within walking distance of Las Olas, it's worth the extra time to find your perfect vacation rental on Vrbo before committing to a neighborhood.

If you are weighing a couple of areas against each other, browse Fort Lauderdale vacation rentals with pools on Vrbo and use the map view to judge the distances for yourself. Once you know roughly where you want to be, find your perfect vacation rental on Vrbo and sort by what matters most to you — pool, parking, walkability.

Best Fort Lauderdale Hotels: Beachfront Picks for 2026

For travelers who want full-service amenities, daily housekeeping, and beachfront access without the logistics of running a private home, Fort Lauderdale's hotel scene has grown up considerably over the past decade. The Ritz-Carlton Fort Lauderdale, a roughly 200-room high-rise directly on the sand near Sunrise Boulevard, remains the benchmark for five-star service in the city, with a spa, an oceanfront pool deck, and one of the stronger restaurant programs on the strip. The Conrad Fort Lauderdale Beach, an all-suite property with close to 290 suites, suits travelers who want extra living space, kitchenettes, and a rooftop pool overlooking the ocean.

For a livelier, design-forward stay, the W Fort Lauderdale, with more than 300 rooms perched where the New River meets the Intracoastal, pairs beach access with a strong cocktail and nightlife scene. Travelers who prefer a smaller, more traditional beachfront resort tend to gravitate toward the Pelican Grand Beach Resort, a roughly 156-room property with a lazy river pool and direct beach access that families like. Further south, the B Ocean Resort offers a larger, mid-century modern property with around 500 rooms and one of the more distinctive pool decks in the city, priced generally below the Ritz-Carlton and Conrad.

Hotel rates in Fort Lauderdale swing hard by season. January through April brings the highest prices, while late summer offers the deepest discounts, sometimes 30 to 40 percent below peak. Booking through a comparison platform rather than a single hotel site tends to surface those swings more clearly. We generally check rates where travelers can save 10 percent or more on hotels with Member Prices before locking in a beachfront property, and it's worth a few minutes to compare hotel deals on Hotels.com across two or three properties in your target neighborhood. Fort Lauderdale's beachfront rates can vary by more than $100 a night for comparable rooms depending on the week you book.

Fort Lauderdale Vacation Rental vs. Beachfront Hotel: Which to Choose

The rental-versus-hotel decision in Fort Lauderdale comes down mostly to group size, length of stay, and how much you value daily service over space and privacy. For a couple staying three or four nights who wants breakfast delivered, a pool bar an elevator ride away, and zero responsibility for towels or trash, a beachfront hotel almost always wins on convenience. The Ritz-Carlton, Conrad, and Pelican Grand Beach Resort each deliver that experience well.

For a family of six, two couples traveling together, or anyone staying a week or longer, the math shifts quickly toward a vacation rental. A three- or four-bedroom canal-front home with a private pool frequently costs less per person per night than the equivalent number of hotel rooms, while adding a full kitchen that can meaningfully cut down on restaurant spending over a longer stay. The trade-off is more self-sufficiency: no daily housekeeping unless you pay for a mid-stay cleaning, no front desk to solve a problem at 11 p.m., and usually a car or reliable rideshare access if the property sits off the main water taxi route.

Our general rule: choose a hotel for stays under five nights or when walkability to the beach and Las Olas is non-negotiable, and choose a rental for longer stays, larger groups, or when a private pool and full kitchen matter more than daily service. Either way, book the neighborhood first and the specific property second. Fort Lauderdale's character shifts meaningfully between the central beach, Lauderdale-by-the-Sea, and Pompano Beach.

Everglades Day Trips from Fort Lauderdale

Basing yourself in Fort Lauderdale puts you surprisingly close to the Everglades, and that's an underrated advantage of staying here rather than further up the coast. Drive west on I-595 to US-27 and most visitors reach the eastern edge of the Everglades in roughly 30 to 40 minutes, which makes it a realistic half-day excursion even if you're also planning beach time the same day.

Everglades Holiday Park and Sawgrass Recreation Park are the two most established airboat operators serving day-trippers from Fort Lauderdale, both offering guided rides through sawgrass marsh with stops to view alligators, wading birds, and, depending on the season, the occasional Burmese python sighting from park naturalists. Book the earliest available morning slot if you can. Wildlife activity peaks before the midday heat, and afternoon thunderstorms are common during the wet season from June through September.

If you'd rather not manage your own driving through unfamiliar backroads, particularly given how limited cell coverage gets past the outskirts of Fort Lauderdale, a private driver for the half-day is a reasonable upgrade, especially for groups splitting the cost across a Cadillac Escalade or Mercedes Sprinter van. It also means no one has to skip the post-tour rum punch stand near the park entrance in order to drive back.

Fort Lauderdale Cruise Port: What to Know Before You Sail

If part of your trip involves boarding a ship at Port Everglades, this stay-focused guide isn't the resource you need for terminal logistics, cruise line itineraries, or cruise parking. We cover all of that in detail, including a suggested one-day pre- or post-cruise itinerary built around Fort Lauderdale's beach and Las Olas, in our dedicated best cruise itineraries from Fort Lauderdale and Miami guide.

What matters here is simply that Port Everglades sits just a few minutes south of the central beach hotel district, which is why many cruisers choose to spend one or two nights in Fort Lauderdale before or after their sailing rather than flying in the same day. If that describes your trip, everything in this guide, from neighborhood selection to the vacation-rental-versus-hotel decision, still applies to those pre- or post-cruise nights. You'll just want to time your checkout and airport or port transfer using the logistics detailed in our cruise-specific guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best area to stay in Fort Lauderdale?

The central Fort Lauderdale Beach strip near Las Olas Boulevard is best for walkability to restaurants and nightlife. Lauderdale-by-the-Sea suits travelers wanting a quieter, small-town beach feel, while Pompano Beach offers similar beach access at generally lower rates.

Is it cheaper to book a vacation rental or a hotel in Fort Lauderdale?

For stays of five nights or longer or groups of four or more, a vacation rental with a private pool and kitchen is typically cheaper per person than an equivalent number of hotel rooms. For shorter stays of two to four nights, a hotel is often comparably priced once cleaning fees are factored in.

How far is Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport from the beach?

FLL sits roughly three miles from downtown Fort Lauderdale and the central beach hotel corridor, typically a 10 to 15 minute drive depending on traffic and which terminal you depart from.

What is the Fort Lauderdale Water Taxi and is it worth it?

The Fort Lauderdale Water Taxi is a hop-on, hop-off boat service running along the New River and Intracoastal Waterway, connecting downtown, Las Olas, the beach, and points toward Hollywood. It is worth booking for at least one day, since it doubles as a scenic tour of the city's canal system and mega-yacht docks.

Is Fort Lauderdale a good base for visiting the Everglades?

Yes. Everglades Holiday Park and Sawgrass Recreation Park are both roughly 30 to 40 minutes west of Fort Lauderdale via I-595 and US-27, making an airboat tour an easy half-day trip from any beach-area hotel or rental.

What is the difference between Fort Lauderdale Beach and Hollywood Beach?

Fort Lauderdale Beach is livelier and denser with hotels and restaurants directly on A1A, while Hollywood Beach, about 20 minutes south, centers on the 2.5-mile Broadwalk promenade and has a quieter, old-Florida character with fewer high-rise resorts.

When is the best time to visit Fort Lauderdale for lower hotel rates?

Late summer, roughly July through September, typically offers the lowest hotel rates, sometimes 30 to 40 percent below the January through April peak season, though this period also carries higher humidity and afternoon thunderstorm risk.

Do I need a car to visit Fort Lauderdale?

Not necessarily if you stay downtown or along the central beach corridor, where the Sun Trolley, water taxi, and rideshare cover most attractions. A car or private driver becomes more useful for trips to the Everglades or the northern beach towns like Pompano Beach.

Is this guide the right resource if I'm taking a cruise from Fort Lauderdale?

This guide focuses on staying in Fort Lauderdale rather than cruise logistics. If you are sailing from Port Everglades, our separate best cruise itineraries from Fort Lauderdale and Miami guide covers terminals, parking, and pre/post-cruise planning in detail.

What is Las Olas Boulevard known for?

Las Olas Boulevard is Fort Lauderdale's main shopping and dining street, roughly one mile long, connecting downtown to the beach and lined with boutiques, galleries, and restaurants, with the residential canal district of the Las Olas Isles just to the south.
